I personally believe Valve could sustain themselves on their trading cards and digital item sales only. Not even take a percentage of game sales and just host the platform for the sales to occur.

You might think that's a questionable statement, but here's some math to show why I think what I think:

On a Steam Sale, the limited edition sale cards sell around 20,000 copies per hour at an average of $0.10 (this information comes from experience I've gained from actively participating in Steam Sales regularly for years).

Valve takes a 10% cut of every sale of a trading card. That's $0.01, but 20,000 times is $200 in 24 hours. That doesn't sound like a lot, but realize that's a single card at the lowest price Valve can get for it. There's a hard limit where even if you sold the card at $0.03, Valve still gets $0.01 (making the final price for the buyer $0.04). The foil (rarer) cards go for about $1 or more, and sell at around 1/20th the volume (as an example), so 1000 times but at $0.10, so another $100 in 24 hours.

Now, assuming millions of cards are sold/bought per day, with the spikes on Sales due to the freebie card you get during them, Valve is easily making $100,000+ on trading cards per day on very very little infrastructure relative to the money gained from it.

But trading cards are the cheap and lowest tier digital money maker. CS:GO has skins; TF2 has hats. Valve takes a portion of every one of those sales as well. The volume is probably not as significant as cards, but the prices are higher generally. Considering some people make $100,000+ per year on Steam selling hats and other digital items (Gabe mentions this while talking about it back in 2012 I think), Valve must make a considerable amount themselves.

All in all, I'd guess Valve makes at least a couple of million dollars per day from their digital item sales alone, if not more.
